results.title: remove_duplicates() keeps duplicates

attribution.claimed_cause: The change in `remove_duplicates` replaced the logical **`or`** with **`and`** in the list‑comprehension condition. The original logic was: ```python row for row in self._data if not (tuple(row) in seen or seen.add(tuple(row))) ``` which keeps a row only when it has not been seen before. The new logic: ```python row for row in self._data if not (tuple(row) in seen and seen.add(tuple(row))) ``` uses `and` instead of `or`, causing the condition to evaluate to `True` for every row, so no duplicates are removed.
evidence_for: The failure shows that `self.founders.height` remains 6 instead of the expected 3, indicating duplicates were not removed.
The diff shows the list‑comprehension condition changed from `or` to `and`.
The original logic `if not (tuple(row) in seen or seen.add(tuple(row)))` correctly skips rows that are already in `seen`.

Replacing `or` with `and` makes the condition `if not (tuple(row) in seen and seen.add(tuple(row)))` always evaluate to `False` for new rows, because `seen.add` returns `None`, so the `and` short‑circuits and the whole expression becomes `False`. Thus the `not` makes it `True` for all rows, keeping every row.
The test expects the dataset to shrink to 3 unique rows, but the dataset remains at 6, matching the behavior of the buggy `and` logic.

results.title: transpose() picks the wrong code path for headers

attribution.claimed_cause: The condition that selects the transpose implementation was inverted. In `Dataset.transpose()` the original logic was: ```python if self.headers is None: return self._transpose_without_headers() else: return self._transpose_with_headers() ``` The patch changed it to: ```python if self.headers is not None: return self._transpose_without_headers() else: return self._transpose_with_headers() ``` Thus when `self.headers` is `None`, the code now incorrectly calls `_transpose_with_headers`, which expects headers to exist and fails.
evidence_for: The failure log shows a `TypeError` in `_transpose_with_headers` where it accesses `self.headers[0]`, implying `self.headers` is `None` at that point.

The test `test_transpose_multiple_headers` calls `data.transpose()` on a dataset with no headers, expecting `_transpose_without_headers()` to be used, but the stack trace shows `_transpose_with_headers()` was called instead.
The diff shows the condition was inverted: `if self.headers is not None:` now triggers `_transpose_without_headers()`, causing the wrong branch to execute when `self.headers` is `None`.

The `test_transpose` failure shows that `transposed_founders.headers` is `None` after transpose, whereas it should contain the original headers, indicating the transpose logic did not preserve headers correctly.

The original logic `if self.headers is None: return self._transpose_without_headers()` correctly selected the header‑less transpose, whereas the patched logic mistakenly selects the header‑aware branch when `self.headers` is `None`.

repairs.patch:
--- a/src/tablib/core.py
+++ b/src/tablib/core.py
@@
-        if self.headers is not None:
-            return self._transpose_without_headers()
-        else:
-            return self._transpose_with_headers()
+        # If the dataset has no headers, use the header‑less transpose.
+        if self.headers is None:
+            return self._transpose_without_headers()
+        else:
+            return self._transpose_with_headers()

results.title: remove_duplicates() keeps duplicates

attribution.claimed_cause: The change in `remove_duplicates` replaced the logical **`or`** with **`and`** in the list‑comprehension condition. The original logic was: ```python row for row in self._data if not (tuple(row) in seen or seen.add(tuple(row))) ``` which keeps a row only when it has not been seen before. The new logic: ```python row for row in self._data if not (tuple(row) in seen and seen.add(tuple(row))) ``` uses `and` instead of `or`, causing the condition to evaluate to `True` for every row, so no duplicates are removed.
evidence_for: The failure shows that `self.founders.height` remains 6 instead of the expected 3, indicating duplicates were not removed.
The diff shows the list‑comprehension condition changed from `or` to `and`.
The original logic `if not (tuple(row) in seen or seen.add(tuple(row)))` correctly skips rows that are already in `seen`.

Replacing `or` with `and` makes the condition `if not (tuple(row) in seen and seen.add(tuple(row)))` always evaluate to `False` for new rows, because `seen.add` returns `None`, so the `and` short‑circuits and the whole expression becomes `False`. Thus the `not` makes it `True` for all rows, keeping every row.
The test expects the dataset to shrink to 3 unique rows, but the dataset remains at 6, matching the behavior of the buggy `and` logic.

repairs.patch:
--- a/src/tablib/core.py
+++ b/src/tablib/core.py
@@
-        self._data[:] = [
-            row for row in self._data if not (tuple(row) in seen and seen.add(tuple(row)))
-        ]
+        self._data[:] = [
+            row for row in self._data if not (tuple(row) in seen or seen.add(tuple(row)))
+        ]

results.title: CSV default delimiter changed to ';'

attribution.claimed_cause: The change of `CSVFormat.DEFAULT_DELIMITER` from a comma (`,`) to a semicolon (`;`) in `src/tablib/formats/_csv.py`.
evidence_for: The `export_stream_set` method in `src/tablib/formats/_csv.py` writes rows using `cls.DEFAULT_DELIMITER`, which is now `';'`, so the exported CSV string contains semicolons instead of commas, matching the assertion failure in `CSVTests.test_csv_export`.

The `detect_format` function relies on the presence of a comma delimiter to recognize CSV files; with the default changed to `';'`, it no longer detects the test CSV data (`_csv`), causing `tablib.detect_format(_csv)` to return `None` and failing `TablibTestCase.test_auto_format_detect`.

The test data in `tests/test_tablib.py` expects a comma‑delimited CSV (e.g., `"first_name,last_name,gpa\r\n..."`), which is no longer produced, directly linking the changed delimiter to the observed mismatches.

The diff shows the only modification in the CSV format file is the line `DEFAULT_DELIMITER = ';'`, indicating no other code paths were altered that could explain the failure, strengthening the causal link.
